consciousness_check.title: Consciousness Assessment
consciousness_check.question: Is the person conscious and responding to you?
consciousness_check.hint: Shout loudly 'Can you hear me? Are you okay?' and firmly tap both shoulders. Observe their reaction.

options.label: No, completely unconscious / unresponsive
options.description: Limp, eyes closed, no reaction to shouting, tapping, or sound.

options.label: Yes, awake and responding, but in distress
options.description: They can speak, nod, open eyes, or move, but need emergency help.

options.label: Not sure / In and out of consciousness
options.description: Drifting off, eyes rolling back, confused, barely responsive or groaning.

unconscious_assessment.title: Unconscious Assessment
unconscious_assessment.question: What do you observe about their breathing or body movement?
unconscious_assessment.hint: Look closely at their chest and body. Look for rhythmic breathing vs gasping or violent jerking.

options.label: Body is shaking violently / stiffening / convulsing
options.description: Jerking limbs, jaw clenched, unresponsive to touch.

advice.title: Active Seizure / Convulsion (Epileptic Fit)
advice.description: The person is having a seizure. Do not panic; most seizures resolve naturally within 2 to 3 minutes. Your primary mission is protecting them from physical trauma.
points: Cushion their head with something soft (a folded jacket, pillow, or hands) to prevent head injury.
Clear away all hard, sharp, or dangerous objects around them.
Loosen tight clothing around their neck (collars, scarves, ties) to aid airflow.
Time the seizure: note the exact minute the shaking began.
Once shaking stops completely, roll them gently onto their side into the Recovery Position to keep airway open.
Call 112 immediately if: seizure lasts > 5 minutes, it is their first seizure, they have breathing trouble afterwards, or they are pregnant or injured.
donts: DO NOT physically restrain or pin down their arms or legs.
DO NOT put anything in their mouth (they cannot swallow their tongue; forcing objects breaks teeth or causes choking).
DO NOT give water, medicine, or food until they are 100% awake and talking.
advice.dispatcherScript: Adult having an active seizure/convulsions. Head cushioned and area cleared. Seizure has lasted approximately [X] minutes. Address: [Location].

options.label: No breathing, or only occasional gasping / choking sounds
options.description: Agonal gasps are a sign of cardiac arrest. Compressions must start immediately.

advice.title: Suspected Cardiac Arrest (Immediate Action)
advice.description: The person is in cardiac arrest. Their heart has stopped pumping blood to the brain. Hands-Only chest compressions must start right now.
points: Call 112 immediately on speakerphone or point at a bystander to call.
Send someone immediately to locate the nearest Automated External Defibrillator (AED).
Position hands in center of chest (between breasts), heel of one hand with fingers interlocked.
Push hard and fast: 2 inches (5 cm) deep at 110 beats per minute. Switch to our interactive CPR Screen for rhythm & timer.
Standard CPR technique is identical for women and men. Good Samaritan laws protect you.
donts: DO NOT waste time checking for a pulse (untrained pulse checks waste critical minutes).
DO NOT wait to see if gasping stops. Gasping is NOT breathing; it is cardiac arrest.
advice.dispatcherScript: Adult collapsed, unresponsive, and not breathing normally. Starting CPR chest compressions. Send an ambulance and AED to [Location].

options.label: Yes, breathing smoothly, normally, and regularly
options.description: Chest rises and falls rhythmically at a normal pace.

advice.title: Unconscious but Breathing (Airway Protection)
advice.description: The person is unresponsive but breathing regularly. Your priority is keeping their airway open and preventing tongue or fluid obstruction.
points: Gently roll them onto their side into the Recovery Position with the top knee bent to prop them up.
Tilt their chin gently upward to ensure the tongue does not block the airway.
Call 112 and report an unconscious person who is breathing.
Stay with them and check breathing every 30 seconds. If breathing stops or turns into gasping, roll onto back and start CPR immediately.
donts: DO NOT leave them lying flat on their back (tongue or fluids can block the airway).
DO NOT shake them violently or slap their face to wake them up.
advice.dispatcherScript: Adult unconscious but breathing normally. Patient placed in recovery position. Address: [Location].

conscious_symptoms.title: Symptom Identification
conscious_symptoms.question: What primary distress is the person experiencing?
conscious_symptoms.hint: Select the symptom that best describes what you observe or what the person reports.

options.label: Choking (clutching throat, silent, unable to speak or cough)
options.description: Object or food completely obstructing the airway.

advice.title: Severe Choking (Complete Airway Obstruction)
advice.description: The person cannot breathe, speak, or cough. Their airway is completely obstructed and brain oxygen is rapidly depleting.
points: Ask: 'Are you choking?' If they nod and cannot speak, reassure them you will help.
Stand slightly behind them. Support their chest with one hand and lean them well forward.
Give up to 5 sharp back blows with the heel of your hand right between the shoulder blades.
If still blocked, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich): place a fist just above their navel, grasp with other hand, and pull sharply inwards and upwards.
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object clears.
If they lose consciousness: lower them gently to the floor, call 112, and start chest compressions immediately.
donts: DO NOT slap their back while they are upright (it can lodge the object deeper).
DO NOT do blind finger sweeps inside their mouth (can push food further down).
DO NOT give them water to drink while choking.
advice.dispatcherScript: Adult choking, airway obstructed, unable to speak. Performing back blows and abdominal thrusts. Address: [Location].

options.label: Crushing chest pain / heavy pressure radiating to arm or jaw
options.description: Awake, sweating, clutching chest, shortness of breath.

advice.title: Suspected Heart Attack (Myocardial Infarction)
advice.description: A heart attack occurs when blood supply to heart muscle is blocked. The person is CONSCIOUS (different from cardiac arrest). Immediate hospitalization is vital.
points: Call 112 immediately. Tell the dispatcher you suspect a heart attack.
Help them sit down comfortably on the floor, leaning back against a wall with knees bent (eases strain on the heart).
Loosen tight clothing around their neck, chest, and waist.
If they have prescribed heart medicine (e.g., Nitroglycerin spray/tablets), assist them in taking it.
If not allergic and not advised against it, ask if they have Aspirin (300 mg to chew slowly).
Keep them calm and quiet. If they suddenly lose consciousness and stop breathing, start CPR immediately.
donts: DO NOT let them walk, drive, or exert physical effort.
DO NOT dismiss symptoms or wait for chest pain to pass.
DO NOT give food or drink other than emergency aspirin.
advice.dispatcherScript: Suspected acute heart attack. Patient is conscious with severe crushing chest pain, sweating, and shortness of breath. Seated comfortably. Address: [Location].

options.label: Face drooping, one arm weak, or slurred / garbled speech
options.description: Sudden onset of neurological symptoms (F.A.S.T. signs).

advice.title: Suspected Stroke (F.A.S.T. Assessment)
advice.description: A stroke occurs when blood flow to brain tissue is interrupted. Every minute saved preserves brain cells ('Time is Brain').
points: Perform the F.A.S.T. check right now:
F — Face: Ask them to smile. Does one side of the mouth or face droop?
A — Arms: Ask them to raise both arms. Does one arm drift downward or feel numb?
S — Speech: Ask them to repeat a simple sentence. Is speech slurred or strange?
T — Time: Call 112 immediately. Note the EXACT time symptoms began (vital for hospital clot-busting medication).
Keep them resting comfortably on their side or seated with head slightly propped up.
donts: DO NOT give Aspirin (if the stroke is caused by bleeding in the brain, aspirin can be fatal).
DO NOT give food, water, or medicine (swallowing muscles may be impaired, causing choking).
DO NOT wait to see if symptoms go away; brain damage progresses rapidly.
advice.dispatcherScript: Suspected acute stroke. F.A.S.T. positive with facial droop and speech difficulty. First noticed at [Exact Time]. Address: [Location].

options.label: Temporarily blacked out, dizzy, pale, but waking back up
options.description: Vasovagal syncope, dehydration, heat, or sudden standing.

advice.title: Fainting / Syncope (Temporary Blackout)
advice.description: Fainting is a temporary drop in blood flow to the brain, usually caused by heat, dehydration, sudden standing, emotional shock, or low blood sugar. Recovery should happen within 1 minute.
points: Keep the person lying flat on their back on a cool, safe surface.
Elevate their legs 12 inches (30 cm) above heart level (propped on a bag or chair) to encourage blood flow back to the brain.
Loosen restrictive collars, belts, or tight clothing.
Ensure plenty of fresh air (ask crowds to step back).
Once fully alert, allow them to sit up slowly. Give water or electrolyte drink only when completely awake.
Call 112 if: they hit their head during the fall, do not regain consciousness within 1 minute, have chest pain, or have a history of heart disease.
donts: DO NOT let them stand up quickly (they will faint again).
DO NOT splash water on their face or slap them.
DO NOT put anything in their mouth while groggy.
advice.dispatcherScript: Person fainted, now conscious and alert. Legs elevated. [State if any head injury occurred]. Address: [Location].

options.label: Severe allergic reaction (swollen lips/tongue, hives, wheezing)
options.description: Reaction to food, medication, or insect sting.

advice.title: Severe Allergic Reaction (Anaphylaxis)
advice.description: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction that constricts airways and causes blood pressure to crash within minutes.
points: Call 112 immediately. State that the person is having severe anaphylaxis.
Ask if they have an Epinephrine Auto-Injector (EpiPen). Help them locate and use it in the outer mid-thigh.
Keep them lying flat with legs raised, UNLESS breathing is difficult (if struggling to breathe, allow them to sit up slightly to ease airflow).
Stay with them. A second dose of epinephrine may be needed after 5–15 minutes if symptoms do not improve.
donts: DO NOT make them stand or walk (sudden posture changes can cause a fatal drop in blood pressure).
DO NOT delay using an auto-injector if available.
advice.dispatcherScript: Severe anaphylactic allergic reaction with airway swelling and breathing difficulty. [EpiPen administered / not available]. Address: [Location].

altered_consciousness_assessment.title: Altered State & Physical Clues
altered_consciousness_assessment.question: What clues or symptoms do you notice about their condition?
altered_consciousness_assessment.hint: Check for sweating, diabetes medical tags, falls or head bumps, extreme heat, or suspected toxins.

options.label: Cold sweating, pale, trembling, or known diabetic
options.description: May be confused, slurring words, hungry, or wearing a medical alert band.

advice.title: Severe Low Blood Sugar (Diabetic Hypoglycemia)
advice.description: The person's blood sugar has dropped dangerously low. The brain is starved of glucose and emergency sugar is needed if they can swallow safely.
points: Check swallowing ability: ONLY if they are awake enough to swallow safely without choking, immediately give 15–20g of fast-acting sugar (fruit juice, sugary soda, 4 glucose tablets, or 2 teaspoons of honey/sugar).
Wait 10–15 minutes for sugar to absorb. If they improve and become fully alert, follow up with a complex snack (biscuits, bread, or a normal meal).
If they are too drowsy to swallow, do NOT force anything into their mouth.
Call 112 immediately if: they cannot swallow, slip into deep unconsciousness, or show no improvement after 10 minutes.
donts: DO NOT force liquids or food down the throat of an unresponsive or semi-conscious person (causes fatal choking/aspiration).
DO NOT administer insulin (insulin drops blood sugar further and can be fatal in hypoglycemia).
advice.dispatcherScript: Diabetic emergency / severe hypoglycemia with altered mental state and cold sweats. [State if sugar was given or unable to swallow]. Address: [Location].

options.label: Recent fall, hit to the head, or visible head/neck injury
options.description: Dazed, nausea, vomiting, confusion, or bleeding from a head bump.

advice.title: Head Injury & Suspected Brain Concussion
advice.description: A hard blow or fall can cause internal brain swelling or bleeding, alongside potential neck/spinal trauma.
points: Keep their head, neck, and spine completely still. Gently hold their head on both sides to prevent twisting.
Do NOT move them unless they are in immediate physical danger (fire, traffic).
If they vomit and are lying down, roll their whole body as one single aligned unit ('log roll') onto their side while supporting the head/neck straight.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth gently to swelling (do not press hard on suspected skull fractures).
Call 112 immediately for any loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, or fluid from ears/nose.
donts: DO NOT twist, bend, or hyperextend their neck.
DO NOT remove a sports helmet unless breathing is blocked and you are trained.
DO NOT give Aspirin or Ibuprofen (they thin blood and worsen internal brain bleeding).
advice.dispatcherScript: Head injury following impact/fall. Patient has fluctuating consciousness, dizziness, and nausea. Head/neck stabilized. Address: [Location].

options.label: Extreme heat exposure, hot dry skin, delirious or staggering
options.description: High temperature, strenuous sun exposure, flushed face, incoherent speech.

advice.title: Heatstroke & Critical Hyperthermia
advice.description: Heatstroke occurs when the body can no longer regulate its internal temperature (>40°C / 104°F), risking rapid organ failure.
points: Call 112 immediately. Inform dispatcher of suspected heatstroke.
Move them into cool shade or air conditioning right away.
Active cooling: loosen and remove heavy clothing. Sponge skin with cool water and fan them vigorously.
Place cool wet cloths or ice packs on areas with major blood vessels: neck, armpits, and groin.
Give small sips of cool water ONLY if they are alert enough to swallow. Do NOT force fluids if they are drifting off.
donts: DO NOT immerse an incoherent or elderly person in an ice bath (can trigger circulatory shock).
DO NOT give fever-reducing tablets like paracetamol (they are ineffective for environmental heatstroke).
advice.dispatcherScript: Suspected acute heatstroke. Patient semi-conscious and delirious with hot skin after heat exposure. Actively cooling in shade. Address: [Location].

options.label: Slow shallow breathing, pinpoint pupils, or suspected poisoning
options.description: Vomiting risk, clammy skin, empty medicine bottles or toxins nearby.

advice.title: Suspected Poisoning / Overdose / Severe Intoxication
advice.description: Toxins and central nervous system depressants slow respiration and threaten airway reflexes.
points: Call 112 immediately. Note any medication bottles, chemical containers, or substances nearby.
If Naloxone (Narcan) is available and an opioid overdose is suspected, administer nasal spray into one nostril immediately.
Place them in the Recovery Position on their side so vomit does not choke their airway.
Monitor breathing continuously. If breathing drops below 8 breaths per minute or stops, start chest compressions immediately.
donts: DO NOT induce vomiting (it can chemically burn the esophagus or flood the lungs).
DO NOT give coffee, lemon juice, or force them into cold showers.
advice.dispatcherScript: Suspected poisoning/overdose with fluctuating consciousness. Patient placed in recovery position, breathing monitored. Address: [Location].

options.label: Recently stopped shaking / slowly waking from a seizure
options.description: Exhausted, confused, groggy, snoring breathing (post-ictal state).

advice.title: Post-Seizure Recovery Phase (Post-Ictal State)
advice.description: After a seizure, the brain takes 5 to 30 minutes to reset. Groggy responses, deep breathing, and temporary confusion are normal.
points: Keep them resting on their side in the Recovery Position.
Reassure them gently as awareness returns: 'You had a seizure, you are safe, I am here.'
Allow them to rest quietly without crowds or bright lights.
Check that they are breathing freely and stay until they are fully oriented (know who and where they are).
Call 112 if they enter another seizure without regaining consciousness, or remain deeply confused > 30 minutes.
donts: DO NOT leave them unattended while still sleepy or unsteady.
DO NOT give food, drink, or oral medication until speech and swallowing are completely normal.
advice.dispatcherScript: Patient in post-ictal recovery after an observed seizure. Conscious but groggy. Resting in recovery position. Address: [Location].
